edges.effect_quant: In 2,350 older NHANES participants, higher total dietary fiber intake was nonlinearly associated with better cognition, with roughly 15 g/day marking the threshold for maximal observed benefit.
edges.population: older adults, including community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older
edges.mechanism: Dietary fiber may support late-life cognition through short-chain-fatty-acid production, improved metabolic and inflammatory tone, and a gut-microbiome profile less likely to amplify neuroimmune stress. Current human evidence is still observational, but it lines up with experimental work linking fermentable fiber to lower inflammatory signaling and better brain resilience.
edges.summary: Higher dietary fiber intake is consistently associated with better cognitive performance in older adults, although the human evidence remains mostly observational rather than interventional. Multiple recent analyses link greater fiber intake to better memory, fluency, or processing-speed performance, supporting a plausible protective role but not yet proving causality.
edges.caveats: The main limitation is confounding: people with higher fiber intake often differ in overall diet quality, education, health status, and activity. Much of the evidence also comes from overlapping U.S. survey datasets, so the confidence is moderate rather than high despite a coherent signal.
